The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026.

Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing.
Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.”

Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.”
During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means.
Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence.
The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices.
When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians.
In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration.
The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan.
Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award.
Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud.
It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices.
The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration.
The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us.

Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan.

items.title: While Russia tries to manipulate information, local civil society is teaching Armenians media literacy

s: A group of journalists and activists created ‘Verify This,’ a platform where users can find reliable information

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Armenia is a small, landlocked country that has, for years, relied on Russian support in its long-term conflict with the neighboring oil-rich and authoritarian country, Azerbaijan.
However, Armenia received a blow from Russia in 2022–2023, when it was not supported by Russian military forces during its conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

In September 2023, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale military offensive, expelled the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh, dissolved the government of the region, and incorporated the territory into Azerbaijan.

After this incident, when Russia did not support Armenia with its peacekeeping troops, likely because Vladimir Putin was already engaged in a full-scale invasion and war with Ukraine, Armenia visibly changed its attitude toward Russia.
Armenian Prime Minister ​Nikol Pashinyan started to work in earnest towards the goal of European Union ⁠membership for his South Caucasus country and increased diplomatic communication with the US.
He was re-elected on June 7, 2026.
The election took place amid reports of Russian interference.

Reuters, citing anonymous Western intelligence officials and documents, reported covert Russian efforts to undermine Pashinyan and support pro-Russian candidates, including through disinformation campaigns.
These elections showed how information warfare has expanded beyond social media.
It now included fake news websites, AI-generated videos and material presented as reporting by reputable international media outlets.
According to the US-based disinformation monitoring organization NewsGuard, a Russia-linked campaign circulated 31 fabricated stories about Pashinyan in just one week.
The stories accused him of election fraud and of trying to drag Armenia into a war with Russia.
Some of this material imitated international media outlets such as France 24 and Politico.
Other stories impersonated Armenian news outlets, including Armenpress and CivilNet.
With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated.
Armenia’s experience shows how these campaigns operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia.
At the same time, Armenian journalists and civil society are working hard to build media literacy to counter disinformation campaigns.
This Digital Spark Spotlight interview is about one of these projects — “ Verify First,” a platform where users can find reliable information.

Global Voices interviewed Armin Asryan, a member of the group of journalists, editors, and activists behind the media literacy project “Verify First,” which tackles Russian information manipulation and propaganda.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Armin Asryan (AA): We are a group of enthusiasts, operating through the ‘Socio Club’ — Social and Information NGO — and dedicated to driving positive change in Armenia’s information landscape.
We chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project because we were thrilled to see an opportunity to actively contribute to a healthier, more reliable information space on social networks.

In response to the growing challenges of online misinformation, we developed a targeted initiative to produce six educational video reels focused on practical fact-checking techniques and media literacy, designed to equip everyday social media users with the tools to spot and counter misleading content.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
AA: The Armenian social media space is heavily impacted by disinformation, low-quality content, and online hostility.
Every day, social media feeds reveal content that not only disappoints users but also generates widespread panic and fear.

items.title: How medical neglect killed Alfredo Díaz in a Venezuelan cell

s: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Illustration made with AI by Runrunes.
Used with permission.
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission.
Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.
To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed.

Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”
Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality.

Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López.
The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.
Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for?
What happens to a report like this once it is published?
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there.

It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims.
This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.
The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide.
That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions.
In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence.
This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.
This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela.
The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression.

The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin.
That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

items.title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence

s: In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.
Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador.

Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center.
The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse.
Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse.
Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents.
Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old.
Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month.

The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million.

The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.
Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest.
Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

items.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional

s: Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional.
Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.
It has been a long road to get to this point.

Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed.
A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”
Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement.
Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council.
He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards.

Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.
With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean.

As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.
It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist.
Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.
The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand.
However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

items.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?

s: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empower community members
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm.
Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon.
Used with permission.
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year.

Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September.

Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families.
Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment.
More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.
Children are among those affected.
Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition.
Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance.
In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.
In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools.

Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.
Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting.
“Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden.
Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.
The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon.
Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.
“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator.
The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf.
Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.
Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience.
Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:
“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said.

“Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

items.title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting

s: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure.
In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law ( HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society.
You can support this coverage by donating here.
Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms.
We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare.
Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.
We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities.

We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.
This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development.
Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration.
It is essential for economic and social infrastructure.
Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability.

With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity.
These investments matter.
But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier?
When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?
Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted.
Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.
For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth.
For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities.
For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.
Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious.

The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.
The scale of the problem is staggering.
The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice.
HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive.
This is a crisis of development.
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.
In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions.
In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.
But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries.
From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.
The consequences extend beyond those directly affected.
When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates.
When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state.
And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge.
Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms.
At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence.
We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

items.title: Restoring social media access comes at a cost in Gabon

s: Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube
After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access.
But it has come at a cost.

This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.

According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.
At first, the suspension had no real impact, with presidential spokesperson Jennyfer Mélodie Sambat claiming it would solely target Meta platforms.

However, according to Gabon Media Time, several influencers, content creators, and citizens later experienced access disruptions on YouTube and TikTok, sometimes rendering connections impossible without a bypass tool, such as a virtual private network (VPN).
The global data platform Internet Society Pulse confirmed this observation, revealing major anomalies for Meta, Telegram, TikTok, and YouTube, but not X (formerly Twitter).
The online news portal Le360 Afrique consequently reported a surge in VPN usage in the months that followed.
For 248 days, more than 1.84 million individuals, or 71.9 percent of the country’s population of over 2.5 million, were denied regular access to some of the world’s most popular digital platforms.
On October 24, 2026, the HAC lifted this suspension, with Africanews stressing that this ruling didn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual.

It, therefore, remains to be seen whether Gabon, where Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema has been president since September 2023, will restore digital freedoms or establish a new state-controlled online model instead.
A new legal framework, enacted on February 26, 2026, underpins this reinstatement.
According to Gabon Media Time, Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 establishes a regulatory framework for digital platform usage, while Ordinance No. 0013/PR/2026 amends the HAC Reorganization Act.

The HAC also invokes a law, enacted on October 5, that ratifies the social media ordinance and establishes a regulatory framework for AI-generated and AI-amplified content, according to reporting by Gabon Review.

What’s more, available data shows that these regulations have introduced joint liability for those who create and share illegal content and require all social media users to provide personal identification information.
Purported as tools to combat abuse, these regulations have raised serious concerns about anonymity, personal data protection, and their stifling effect on public debate.
In a country where criticizing public institutions is politically sensitive, the threat of prosecution for posting online could discourage users from expressing dissent.
The issue here isn’t whether the state should combat cyberbullying, disinformation, or hate speech, but rather how.
While these are valid concerns, the real worry is whether its measures are transparent, proportionate, and subject to independent scrutiny.
The most decisive development in this saga was undoubtedly the unprecedented cooperation between the government and Big Tech companies.
On July 13, 2026, after a meeting at the AI for Good/ WSIS summit in Geneva, Gabonese Minister of Digital Economy Mark-Alexandre Doumba announced an agreement with TikTok.
Both parties signed a 12-month cooperation agreement, ensuring the platform’s compliance with Gabon’s new regulatory framework.
At the meeting, TikTok presented its Q1 2026 content moderation results, revealing that it had removed more than 23,500 pieces of sensitive content in Gabon.
Meanwhile, the HAC confirmed that it had established an “active cooperation” with TikTok, Meta, and YouTube to “improve content moderation.
The regulator added that, during the suspension, it also held direct discussions with these companies.
However, neither the technical details of these exchanges nor the practical operation of the authorities’ reporting tools has been specified.

items.title: In Ukraine, youth are finding their voices in the digital democracy

s: Participants of the Voices of Democracy project in Kyiv, Ukraine.
Photo by beYOUnd.
Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

The war in Ukraine has created a myriad of challenges for youth and their participation in public life and democratic processes, bringing displacement and misinformation as well as decreased opportunities for political engagement, economic activity, and access to information.
At the same time, there are still avenues youth can pursue to contribute to political decisions and shape the fate of their communities.
Despite the war, people can still submit petitions, participate in public consultations, or advocate for their needs online, but there is a lack of awareness about such opportunities.
Furthermore, vulnerable groups — including displaced persons, minorities, and rural communities — know they have a voice, but struggle to find it.

In 2026, the local non-governmental organization beYOUnd implemented a project to help youth from vulnerable groups acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to find their voices in this new era of digital democracy.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Yevheniia Holovenko, the chairwoman of beYOUnd, to learn more about their initiative.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.
Yevheniia Holovenko (YH): beYOUnd is a youth-led NGO based in Ukraine, registered in October 2025, though we’ve worked as a team long before that.

Our mission is to increase the involvement of vulnerable youth, especially internally displaced people and young people facing difficult social and economic circumstances, in integration, self-realization, and civic life.
Our name reflects our philosophy: it starts with you; it goes beyond!
Our team is largely made up of young people who’ve lived through the same challenges as the youth we work with, which shapes how we approach everything we do.
We joined the Digital Sparks initiative because digital democracy and civic space are exactly where Ukrainian youth need support right now.
Safe, informed participation online is inseparable from resilience during war, and it matched our mission perfectly.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

YH: The war has pushed many young Ukrainians, especially internally displaced persons (IDPs), into digital spaces to stay connected, informed, and civically active, often without the tools to do so safely.
We saw a gap: young people were consuming information and even participating online, but without media literacy, digital security awareness, or confidence that their voice could shape anything.
We wanted to close this gap by developing practical digital safety and civic participation skills in displaced and marginalized youth.
We wanted to give them an opportunity to share ideas on how to increase awareness of digital democracy with the involvement of young people in Ukraine.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
YH: Within the project “Voices of Democracy in the Digital Era,” we ran an awareness campaign covering digital security, e-participation, and disinformation, which reached over 8,500 views.
On the education side, we delivered three webinars and three workshops on digital democracy, media literacy, civic action planning, and cybersecurity, engaging over a hundred participants.

We also organized an offline networking event in the capital, Kyiv, bringing 27 participants together in person to connect around these same topics, and build on the online learning with real, face-to-face relationships and exchange.

items.title: Ex-lawmaker sentenced to 12.5 years in prison in closed-door trial in Macau

s: Au Kam San's international legal representative called the trial a ‘sham’ with ‘manufactured allegations’
The Chinese territory of Macau recorded its first conviction under the city’s national security law on November 6, 2026, sentencing 69-year-old former lawmaker Au Kam San to 12.5 years in prison.

The Macau Court of First Instance tried the case behind closed doors, and international observers and rights groups have criticized the verdict, calling it a “ bogus prosecution ” that included “serious violations of his right to a fair trial.
The case raises broader questions about how justice is carried out in Macau, and whether its courts offer a fair, open way to challenge the state.
Au served in Macau’s legislature for over 20 years and remained an outspoken current affairs commentator after his retirement in 2021.
He was convicted on one count of subverting state power, three counts of contacting foreign organizations to endanger national security, and one count of violating confidentiality.
According to the court’s statement, the closed-door trial was held on September 16 and 18.
Au was prosecuted under Macau’s domestic security law, enacted on March 3, 2009, and tightened in 2023.

He was accused of cooperating with hostile foreign organizations to collect and disseminate “numerous political propositions that were clearly permeated with [the intent of] subversion of state power” and to assist in the collection and dissemination of false information that intended to incite hatred against the central government, overthrow and undermine the fundamental national system established by the Chinese Constitution, cause foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macau, and disrupt the Macau Chief Executive election in 2024.
Au’s family members, several media outlets, and dozens of citizens attended the court’s public sentencing.

Au’s wife, Cheng Miu-shan, responded to the sentencing with an open letter, stating that the closed-door hearing and public sentencing were politically motivated and a baseless persecution to humiliate and smear her husband’s character.
Au’s daughter, Cherry Au, defended her father’s innocence in her interview with UK-based media outlet, the Independent:
“What saddens me the most is seeing him being portrayed as a villain by the very government that he served for so many years,” she said.
“I hope people remember the person they knew throughout his career, the reason why they placed their trust in him and elected him time and again.
Right now he is facing profound injustice.
I hope those who remember his years of service will stand by him.”
Au Kam San has been detained since his arrest in July 2025.

He was initially charged with three counts of “subverting state power,” three counts of “establishing contacts with organizations, groups or individuals outside the Macau Special Administrative Region to commit acts that endanger national security,” and one count of “violating confidentiality.
The court reduced the subversion charge to one count after the closed-door hearing.

After the public sentencing, the court issued a press release stressing that it appointed a lawyer to defend Au and that during the trial, Au did not dispute most of the facts and acknowledged that his collusion with and conspiracy with multiple overseas organizations constituted a crime.
It also pointed out that Au did not stop colluding with foreign and overseas organizations to subvert state power after the 2023 amendment of Macau national security law.
The amendment has expanded the definition of subversive acts from “violent means” to “any illegal means,” to more closely align with Hong Kong’s 2020 version of national security law.
However, Au’s daughter told the press that her father had been barred from contacting his family and accessing a private lawyer to represent him in court.

items.title: From a quiet life to the terror of armed gangs: The story of Haiti’s Kenscoff district

s: On October 19, a unit of Salvadoran soldiers was also ambushed; the situation remains tense
View of the hills from the road from Port-au-Prince to Kenscoff.
Photo by Ketounette via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 3.0 ).
In the heights of Pétion-Ville, more than 1,500 metres above sea level, sits the municipality of Kenscoff.
A rural area just 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) southeast of downtown Port-au-Prince, Kenscoff is an idyllic contradiction of sorts.

Its breathtaking landscape is dominated by pine trees and mountain ridges, dotted with terraced gardens and agricultural fields that supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Port-au-Prince markets, grocery chains and restaurants.
Yet, because of its high elevation, it can also get very cold and foggy, with the sun often setting by five in the afternoon.

The majority of Kenscoff’s residents are peasant farmers, though some wealthy Haitians, craving more peace, quiet, and fresh air, have chosen to leave the nearby urban areas of Port-au-Prince and Pétion-Ville for the area’s pastoral charm and community spirit.
Kenscoff was famous for hosting recreational events where people would come to spend the day, eat fritay (fried foods), ride horses, and visit Fort Jacques, the area’s main historic site.

Visitors would also frequent Ranch le Montcel — now temporarily closed ( burned during gang violence in 2025) — and Chalet Le Refuge, a once popular recreational, social and dining centre, now also closed.

But that was a different Kenscoff, before armed gangs attacked the town in two deadly attacks this year — July 7–8 and August 23–24 — burning down houses, killing 164 people, and kidnapping and displacing others.
Like many other regions in the country, the Kenscoff community suddenly turned from peaceful daily living into being held to ransom by criminal elements.

It all began about two years ago, when the area began to be disrupted by gangs’ attempts to invade the mountains and establish bases there, foiled by the vigilance of residents’ self-defence brigades, with the help of the Haitian police and army.
Yet, every time these attacks occurred, several civilians would be killed, while others abandoned their homes, seeking refuge in the centre of Pétion-Ville, which was less exposed to gang violence.

According to a report by the National Human Rights Defense Network (RNDDH) on the two massacres, the apathy shown by the government and high-ranking security officials, despite warnings, contributed to the scale of the losses.

On September 18, close to a month after the second attack, lawyer, human rights activist and RNDDH Programme Director Rosy Auguste Ducéna detailed what happened during her appearance on the show Se Sa NOU VLE, hosted by Rudy Thomas Sanon on the Team Rudy Officiel YouTube channel.

For its investigation, she said, the RNDDH collected testimonies from various local authorities, including the interim mayor and his deputy chief of staff, the justice of the peace (District judge) and his deputy, the police chief, police officers, members of self-defence brigades, and about 100 victims and their relatives who managed to survive.
But these two massacres were not Kenscoff’s first experience with this type of violence.
The town suffered its first attack from January 27 to 29, 2025, forcing many people to flee to the Kenscoff town hall to find shelter.
There they stayed until Easter 2026, when the interim mayor relocated them to the Afè Nèg Konbit school in the Robin area, which was considered relatively safe.
As the terror of July 7-8 later proved, Ducéna said, this turned out to be a false sense of security:

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules

s: This past Friday, Justice Paul Smith of the Supreme Court of Queensland ruled that the City of Moreton Bay Council, immediately north of Brisbane, Australia, acted unlawfully when it removed several homeless people camping in public parks last year.

The court concluded the Council breached the law by providing insufficient time for the homeless people to find alternative accommodation and by disposing of their personal belongings without consent.

In the judgement, Justice Smith said the Council made "errors of law" finding that the Council's seizure and disposal of the property of eight homeless people at Eddie Hyland Park — including their tents and other personal belongings — without consent in April and May last year violated human rights.
Although the eviction involved eight campers at the park, the legal case was brought by eleven applicants who said they were affected by the Council's enforcement actions.
The judgement noted that the Council would still be allowed to remove campers from public parks provided this was done "lawfully".
On Friday, the Council published a statement noting that eight homeless people had taken the Council to court and linking to the Supreme Court judgement.
In that statement Council stated it would continue enforcing its ban on camping on public land.
Responsibility for providing shelter to homeless people rested with the Queensland state government according to the Council.
The court scheduled the next hearing in three weeks to determine relief and costs.
Basic Rights Queensland and the Queensland Human Rights Commission supported the campers in the legal proceedings.
The Council's actions followed its decision earlier in February last year to ban camping on public land, which made camping illegal on public land within the Council from March 12, 2025.

items.title: Australia grants refuge to five Iranian women's national soccer team players

s: Early Tuesday morning, Australia government officials issued humanitarian visas to five members of Iran's national women's football team.

The players refused to sing the Iranian anthem while at the Women's Asian Cup last week. if the visas had not been granted, the five players potentially faced serious punishment on their return to Iran, as Iranian media has labeled them "traitors".
Tony Burke, Minister for Home Affairs of Australia, sent a message on X on Tuesday stating that the five players were "welcome to stay in Australia, to be safe and have a home here".
The players are Zahra Ghanbari (captain), Fatemeh Pasandideh, Zahra Sarbali, Atefeh Ramezanizadeh, and Mona Hamoudi.
Tuesday afternoon, however, the rest of the Iranian national women's soccer team travelled to Gold Coast airport by bus.
As of Tuesday morning, authorities said these remaining Iranian women's soccer team members had not requested asylum, though were welcomed to do so.
Protesters surrounded the bus and some were lying on the ground to stop the bus, and had to be moved by police.

Due to reported threats from Iranian media and officials, in Australia, local police worked with the authorities and provided a safe place for the players to stay, as well as increased presence when the players were traveling.

items.title: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Julio Teherán retires

s: Julio Teherán, a two-time Major League Baseball All-Star, announced his retirement from baseball on Monday, at the age of 35.
The decision came two days after he was scratched from a scheduled start for Team Colombia in the 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) due to a shoulder injury.
Teherán had helped Team Colombia secure a 3-1 victory over Team Panama in the WBC before announcing his retirement.
Teherán had a thirteen-year MLB career, during which he primarily played for the Atlanta Braves, but also played for the Los Angeles Angels, Detroit Tigers, Milwaukee Brewers, and New York Mets.
He made his MLB debut with the Braves in 2011 at the age of 20 and spent his first nine seasons with the team, earning All-Star selections in 2014 and 2016.
Over his MLB career, Teherán compiled a 81-82 record, with a 3.85 ERA, 1.223 WHIP, and 1,260 strikeouts in 1,470.2 innings.
He had spent the 2022 and 2025 seasons playing in the Mexican Baseball League.

items.title: PM of Australia sends E-7A Wedgetail and air-to-air missiles to UAE

s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that, in response to United Arab Emirates call for help, Australia would deploy E-7A Wedgetail, a long-range reconnaissance plane, to help Gulf Arab states defend against attacks from Iran.
The Australian Defence Force said the plane is able to survey four million square kilometers with a powerful radar.
Government officials said the plane would be manned by around 85 Australian defence force (ADF) personnel.
Additionally, Australia would supply middle range air to air missiles, at the request of United Arab Emirates, that could down enemy's drones.
Foreign affairs correspondent at ABC News, Stephen Dziedzic, published a piece on Wednesday noting that from a legal perspective, Australia is at war.
He stated that not being an attacker, and not entering Iran, did not preclude Australia from joining a war.

The correspondent referenced article 51 from United Nations charter about "collective self-defence", which could involve, for example, providing support or intelligence to one of the participants of a war.
The correspondent raised concern that move could make Australia a potential target for attacks from, for example, Iran.

items.title: NSW government proposes rezoning to create residences midway between Sydney and Parramatta

s: The government of New South Wales (NSW), Australia announced plans to rezone the 113-hectare Burwood North precinct this Tuesday.
The plan included building 18,300 new homes in the area, and building a new metro station.
This would position the area as a residential hub between Sydney CBD and Parramatta, shortening commute times down to ten minutes, the proposal said.

With allowance for up to 42 storey residential buildings, the government proposal involved a requirement that at least 5% of the new homes were "affordable housing", offered at a lower rental price to lower income households.
Burwood North Station, scheduled to open in 2032, would provide easier access to retail outlets and businesses located near Parramatta Road, and reduce load on existing train and bus networks.
The proposal text noted it would create 3,900 new jobs to implement the changes.
The proposal was a part of Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy.
The NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was listed as a contact for inquiries and feedback.

items.title: US president Donald Trump demands the unconditional surrender of Iran

s: Last Friday, United States President Donald Trump demanded the "unconditional surrender" of Iran via his Truth Social platform.
The declaration came as the war in Iran had gone on for a week.
Trump has also demanded more "acceptable" leadership in the country.
Trump wrote that once "acceptable" leadership was selected in Iran, the US and its allies would make Iran "economically bigger, better, and stronger than ever before."
On Saturday, in an address to the nation, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Trump's demand is a "dream they should send to their grave."
A week ago, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and killed various government officials, including the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, in strikes.
In retaliation for the attacks, Iran has bombed Middle Eastern countries including Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, according to SBS News.
In the Saturday address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for attacks on regional countries, Jakarta Globe reported.
The Globe also reported that 1,230 people were killed in Iran and that six US troops were killed.
Leavitt has stated that the war would likely last four to six weeks.

items.title: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

s: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday.
As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas.
This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.
The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards.
With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia.
One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged.
As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas.

He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.
In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively.
These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member.
Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.

items.title: Caloundra win round 3 game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra have won their round 3 Football Queensland Premier League 2 game against Pine Hills 5 goals to 2 at Meridan Plains, Queensland, Australia on Sunday.
"Two [wins] from three [games]" said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"I think we'll probably be in the top four now.
Not a bad start.
It's still very early days.
Yeah, you can't get too ahead of yourselves.
I think you've just got to take it week by week for the moment."
Riley Campbell opened the scoring for Caloundra in the second minute.
Aaron Doherty levelled the score two minutes later.
Alex Witte took Pine Hills ahead in the eleventh minute.
Darryl Barton brought the scores level again in the thirteenth minute.
Barton scored his second goal to retake the lead do Caloundra in the twenty seventh minute.
Caloundra lead three goals to two at the break.
Jake Debbage added Caloundra's fourth in the fifty first minute before Mackenar Bradfield took the score line to five goals to three in the ninetieth minute.
"It was a pretty even game, first half," said Pine Hills assistant coach Daniel Cunha.
"[We] conceded three goals.
Lazy goals, in our opinion.
But we managed to bounce back with two goals.
Managed to stay in the game, but yeah, second half with early, conceded early goals, so that was it for us."
Caloundra host Mitchellton on Saturday, while Pine Hills travel to Samford.

items.title: "One Battle After Another" wins 6 Oscars including Best Picture

s: One Battle After Another was the big winner at the 98th Academy Awards ceremony, held on Sunday, March 15 at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, California.
The film received six Oscars including Best Picture.
Director Paul Thomas Anderson personally won Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay, in addition to being one of the producers who received the Best Picture award.

The other three Oscars which One Battle After Another received were for Best Editing and Best Casting, the first time the latter award has been presented, and for Sean Penn as Best Supporting Actor, the third Oscar of his career.
Sinners, which had set a record by earning sixteen Oscar nominations, won awards in four categories: Best Actor for Michael B.
Jordan, Best Original Screenplay for Ryan Coogler, Best Original Score for Ludwig Goransson, and Best Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw.
Arkapaw is the first woman to win an Academy Award for Best Cinematography.
Two other films won multiple Oscars.
Frankenstein won Best Production Design, Best Costume Design, and Best Makeup and Hairstyling.
KPop Demon Hunters won Best Animated Feature and Best Song for Golden.
Best Supporting Actress: Amy Madigan for Weapons
Best International Feature: Sentimental Value, from Norway (directed by Joachim Trier)
Best Visual Effects: Avatar: Fire and Ash
Best Documentary Feature: Mr. Nobody Against Putin
Best Documentary Short: All the Empty Rooms
Best Animated Short: The Girl Who Cried Pearls
Best Live Action Short: The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva (tie)
The Oscar ceremony was hosted by Conan O'Brien.

items.title: South Korean military halts small firearms drills after stray bullet strikes young girl on playground

s: On Tuesday, officials for the South Korean Army said at a press conference that they were suspending all scheduled drills involving smaller firearms such as rifles and handguns.

The decision was made in response to an incident earlier in the week on Monday that resulted in a young girl at a children playground in Daegu being injured near the neck by an alleged stray bullet from a military drill at nearby military facility.
Her injuries were not life-threatening and she was released from the hospital.
Her name was not released to the general public.
Investigations into the circumstances leading up the incident were said to be underway.
The incident raised questions regarding the military's practice of conducting shooting drills in close proximity to civilian territory.
A spokesperson for the army confirmed that a firearms drill had indeed been taking place at the same time the girl reported being struck.
The incident came a year after the South Korean Army accidentally bombed a small village near the North Korean border, injuring 30 civilians, while conducting a drill with US forces.

items.title: Musique Libre Femmes plays for Women's History Month at Tompkins Square Library in New York City

s: On Thursday, March 12, 2026, the Tompkins Square Library in New York City hosted a concert by Musique Libre Femmes, in its basement performance space.
This performance featured Cheryl Pyle on flute, Ayumi Ishito on saxophones, and Roberta Piket on piano.
There were approximately fifteen people in attendance.
Wikinews attended the event and took several photos and recordings to transcribe for this news report.
The performance started at 6:00 p.m.
New York Time (2200 UTC), and was introduced by director of adult services Jeffrey Katz.
After explaining that the series was ongoing, and announcing upcoming performance dates as well, he introduced the performers:
((Jeffrey Katz)) So we are celebrating Women's History Month with Musique Libre Femmes.
And this is a group of all women free jazz improvisers who compose, create spontaneous, in-the-moment music.
The group consists of some of the most experienced improvisers of the New York Jazz scene.
And they have recently played at the Lady Got Chops Festival, the Downtown Music Gallery, and many of the New York City Jazz venues.
After which, the performance began and lasted about forty minutes, after which the audience applauded.
After the event, Pyle had the following comments about the series:

((Cheryl Pyle)) I started the group Musique Libre Femmes, Free Music Women, because I saw a film called Fire Music, and they interviewed Carla Bley and Ingrid Sertso, and they didn't talk about any of their music.
And they didn't talk about any other women improvisers, Barbara Donald, you know, anybody.
So I wanted to do some concerts with all women.
((CP)) And today we played with Roberta Piket on piano and Ayumi Ishito on tenor sax and soprano sax and myself, Cheryl Pyle on C-flute, piccolo and alto flute.
And we're here at the Tompkins Square Library in the East Village and we just had a wonderful concert.

items.title: United States announces blockade on the Strait of Hormuz

s: On Sunday, United States President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that the US is imposing a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Trump, the blockade was in effect as of 10:00 a.m.
Eastern Time (1400 UTC).
The blockade was imposed following the collapse of talks held in Islamabad between the United States and Iran.
"Effective immediately, the United States Navy, the finest in the world, will be BLOCKADING any and all ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz," Trump declared.
According to The Guardian, oil prices briefly rose above US$100 a barrel following news of the blockade, before easing back to just over US$99; gas prices also increased.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf posted on X to "Enjoy the current pump figures.
With the so-called 'blockade', soon you'll be nostalgic for $4–$5 gas.
He further stated that Iran would respond in kind to both escalation and diplomacy, warning that it would "fight" if confronted militarily but would "deal with logic" if approached constructively.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed hope that the ceasefire would remain stable, stating that Beijing is willing to cooperate with all parties to "guarantee the uninterrupted flow of energy supplies," and that stability in the Strait of Hormuz is critically important to China.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV visits four nations in Africa

s: Pope Leo XIV arrived by plane in Algeria on Monday, April 13, beginning his apostolic visit to Africa.

A senior Vatican official told the BBC the pope wanted to "turn the world's attention to Africa"; the BBC reported the eleven-day visit would address themes of peace, migration, and interfaith dialogue.
The trip also includes stops in Cameroon, Angola, and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit marked Leo's second major foreign trip as pope since his election in May last year.
The regions of the continent being visited are among the quickest growing in Catholicism in the world.
There were an estimated 288 million Catholics in Africa in 2024, making up more than one-fifth of the world's total.
His first stop in Algeria marked the first papal visit to the country in history.
While there, Leo planned to visit several locations including ancient Christian sites in Annaba and the Great Mosque of Algiers in the capital before departing.

The stop was followed by a visit to Cameroon, where Leo addressed about 120,000 people in Douala, encouraging young people to turn away from violence and corruption and advocating for justice and peace.
He was expected to make a planned visit to a Catholic hospital in the city before traveling to Yaoundé to meet with students from the Catholic University of Central Africa.
On Sunday, April 19, the pope arrived in Angola, where he met with President João Lourenço and other officials.
He later addressed a crowd gathered near the capital, Luanda.
He was also expected to visit the town of Muxima, the country's main Christian pilgrimage site.

After Angola, the pope arrived on Tuesday, April 21, in Equatorial Guinea, where, according to the BBC, Catholics make up more than 70% of the central African nation, for the final leg of the visit, before his scheduled return to the Vatican.

items.title: Wikimedia Foundation closes Wikinews after 21 years

s: The Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation announced on March 30 its decision to close all language editions of the project.

In the announcement, a representative from Wikimedia Foundation cited motivations such as "long-term sustainability, levels of community activity, and the availability of reliable news coverage on other platforms".
The announcement stated that all Wikinews editions—referring to the multiple language sections of Wikinews—would "transition to read-only mode" on May 4.
The announcement did not mention the time zone when the wiki would go in read-only mode; but Wikinews operated under the UTC timezone.

In the announcement message, WMF trustee Victoria Doronina said, "We thank all contributors who have participated in Wikinews over the years and helped build a unique experiment in collaborative journalism within the Wikimedia movement.
We understand that some of them may be disappointed by this decision.
To our regret, the project wasn't able to fulfil its promise, and many of its functions were eclipsed by the notable news coverage in Wikipedias."
According to the WMF, most traffic to Wikinews came in the form of web crawlers and bots, as opposed to humans.
Per the Wikimedia Cloud statistics in the past one year, both, English and Chinese Wikinews received more traffic from humans as compared to crawlers.
The foundation stated in its closure recommendation that it is "difficult to claim that it is disseminating educational content and, even more so, that it is doing so effectively and globally."
On March 31, users from different countries and regions started discussions regarding moving the Wikinews content and community to another website at Wikimedia's Meta-Wiki.

Miraheze and Wikimedia NYC were in discussion of continuing the hosting as Wikinews Pulse, with a restructure to increase multilingual support and try new outputs, according to a note by a Wikimedia volunteer User:Pharos.
However, at the time of publishing this report, they had not provided an estimated time the project would be restarted.
Wikinews was a sister project of other Wikimedia initiatives.
Some of the other sister projects includes Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wikimedia Commons.
All of these Wikimedia projects support the dissemination of free knowledge and media.
The future of Wikinews was raised for consideration in June, with a WMF task force recommending the project's closure, followed by a period of public consultation about Wikinews.
After this process, the Board announced in March that the 31 active editions of Wikinews would be placed in read-only mode indefinitely.
Wikinews was launched in November 2004.
It was first proposed by an anonymous contributor in January 2003 and faced a community vote that ended 151 yea and 59 nay, leading to the first demo going live in October 2004.
The English-language Wikinews was formally created December 2 of that year, with German following one day later.
The project's early development followed a series of community discussions and milestones in late 2004 and early 2005.
A non-binding straw poll on content licensing began on October 26, 2004, alongside discussions on the project's scope and policies.
The initial demo site, hosted at demo.wikinews.org, was later moved to the English Wikinews domain on December 2 of that year.

Following the launch of the English and German editions in December 2004, additional language editions were created in early 2005, including Dutch, French, Swedish, Spanish, Bulgarian, Polish, Romanian, and Portuguese.
The project also adopted a logo in February 2005 through a community voting process.
While many Wikinews articles were synthesized from other news sources, the project also posted original reporting.
The purpose of this activity was to add exclusive content which would not be available elsewhere on the web or on television.
These original reports included interviews with people such as Shimon Peres, then-president of Israel; U.S.
Senator Sam Brownback; journalist Gay Talese; and voice actor Billy West.
A 2005 article featuring original reporting, Unrest in Belize, was cited by Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales as Wikinews's first scoop.

items.title: Opposition leader Tarique Rahman returns to Bangladesh after 17 years

s: Tarique Rahman, the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, landing in Dhaka after 17 years in self-imposed exile in London.
His arrival marks a significant development in the country's political landscape following the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.
Rahman is the son of Khaleda Zia, the official chairperson of the party and former Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
Upon landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Rahman was greeted by thousands of Bangladesh Nationalist Party supporters amid tight security.

Accompanied by his wife, Zubaida Rahman, and daughter, Zaima Rahman, he addressed a rally, emphasizing national unity, inclusivity across religious lines, and the vision of a democratic and economically strong Bangladesh.
He drew parallels to the country's 1971 war of independence.
Rahman, aged 60, left Bangladesh in 2008 for medical treatment after being released on bail following 18 months in detention during the military-backed government's rule from 2006 to 2008.
He was convicted in absentia of charges including corruption, money laundering, and involvement in a 2004 grenade attack on a political rally for his political rival, Sheikh Hasina.
These convictions were overturned or stayed after Hasina's government's fall.
His return comes amid preparations for general elections scheduled for early 2026, under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.
The elections follow a student-led uprising in 2024 that resulted in Hasina's removal and her subsequent flight to India.
The protests, initially sparked by opposition to a job quota system, escalated into broader anti-government demonstrations, leading to an estimated 1,400 deaths according to United Nations figures.
Hasina has since been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the crackdown.
According to a December poll by the International Republican Institute, the BNP is the frontrunner for the election with 30 percent support.
The party has recently distanced itself from allies like Jamaat-e-Islami to adopt a more centrist approach.
However, challenges remain, including integrating party factions, maintaining law and order, and addressing potential unrest from Awami League supporters.
The Awami League was not allowed to participate in the elections.
Rahman's mother, Khaleda Zia, 80, is hospitalised in critical condition since November 2025.
She was the BNP's acting chairman since 2018 and was jailed most of the times during Hasina's administration.

items.title: United States capture Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro

s: The president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, has been captured by the United States on Saturday at around 3 am UTC-4, according to a post by US president Donald Trump on social media.
Trump has told reporters Maduro had been “in a house that was more like a fortress”, in the country’s capital, Caracas.
Trump justified this action by claiming that Maduro is the leader of the Cartel de los Soles, and pushing illegal immigration of dangerous individuals in the United States.
Yván Gil Pinto, Venezuela’s foreign minister, said the country has requested a United Nations Security Council meeting to be held after the attack.
The BBC reports airstrikes in Caracas targeting La Carlota, an airbase and Fort Tiuna, a military base where the United States suspected Maduro to be located, and in other locations.
According to local authorities there has been civilian deaths and injuries, but the exact numbers are still unknown.
It was also reported by the BBC that the operation was orchestrated by a {CIA infiltration of the Venezuelan government.
France 24 reported that the CIA had been monitoring his “every movement since August”, despite Maduro’s efforts to change location regularly.
It was also reported that the operation involved more than 150 military aircraft, including one helicopter that was to capture Maduro.

According to the United States authorities, the Delta Force special operation force, arrived at Maduro’s location at “2:01 a.m. local time” and were able to capture him before he could get into his solid steel safe room (sources contradict however, on his exact location at that point.
Some sources reported that Trump said Maduro was almost in his safe room whilst others said he was sleeping in his bed).
They then relocated the “indicted persons” on a ship after crossing the coastline of Venezuela at 3:29 am.

Trump later revealed that Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, was also captured, and both were on board the USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) with destination the southern district of New York, ultimately to be prosecuted.

Attorney General Pam Bondi was quoted by the BBC saying “[he will] face the full wrath of American justice on American soil in American courts” and, according to CNN, announced an indictment for leading “state‐sponsored gangs” and supporting drug trafficking.
Venezuelan authorities also reported other strikes, said to be made with the intent of seizing their oil and minerals, and have declared national emergency.
They, along with Cuba, Colombia, Iran and Russia, have denounced the action as a “serious military aggression”.
Argentine’s president, Javier Milei supported the action.
Venezuela’s vice‐president, Delcy Rodríguez called for Maduro and his wife to be released, saying the operation violated the country’s territorial integrity.
The BBC stated that these strikes follow a string of more than 30 strikes on Venezuelan vessels, and a strike on a “dock area” in Maracaibo, resulting in the death of more than 110 people.
The Trump administration stated that it is engaging in “non‐international armed conflict with […] alleged drug traffickers”.
According to the BBC, legal experts doubt the legality of these actions, saying the strikes are not against "lawful military targets".
According to CNN, Trump also justified not advising Congress before the operation to avoid a "leak", which drew criticisms from Democratic lawmakers.

After the capture, the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment against Maduro in which Maduro and others were charged with “conspiracy to commit narco‐terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine”.

According to the BBC, Maduro has denied this and has said before that Trump’s actual goal is to get access to Venezuela’s oil reserves, as indicated by the United States’ confiscation of several oil tankers.

items.title: Kyiv street to be named for former Ukrainian parliament chairman Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv

s: A street in Kyiv will be named after the former Speaker of the Parliament Andriy Parubiy, killed in Lviv.
The initiative to commemorate the prominent Ukrainian politician was supported by 57% of participants in a public poll on "Kyiv Digital" application.
On January 1, Maryna Poroshenko, the leader of “European Solidarity”, announced the street name in the Kyiv City Council and on Facebook.
As the result, a section along Mariinsky Park – from Hrushevskoho Street to Parkova Road – will bear the politician's name, named "Andrei Parubia Street".
In December, former President of Ukraine and head of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko asked the residents of Kyiv to support the vote to name the street after Parubiy.
The street had no name at the time of the proposal.
"This place is significant for our team and for Andriy himself — a significant part of his journey is connected with it," Poroshenko said.
On October 1, 2025, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree awarding Parubiy the title of Hero of Ukraine.

A petition to award the title of Hero of Ukraine to Parubiy was registered on the presidential website on September 2, gaining 25,000 signatures, which was necessary for the proposal to be considered by President.
The Verkhovna Rada, the Ukrainian parliament, also supported the request.
Parubiy was among several people who were conferred Heroes of Ukraine.
Others were writer Volodymyr Vakulenko and student and footballer Stepan Chubenko.
Poroshenko lauded the decision, recalling that "Parubiy dedicated his entire life to serving Ukraine".
Andriy Parubiy, 54, who served as the Chairman of Verkhovna Rada from 14 April 2016 to 29 August 2019, was shot and killed in Lviv on 30 August 2025.
He died at the scene from injuries.
The killing happened amid the Russian invasion, which started in 2022.
The shooter managed to escape.
Later, Ukrainian authorities detained a suspect, and allege there is a Russian link to the killing.
Parubiy was an active participant of Euromaidan.
He also served as Secretary of the National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine from February till August 2014.
The suspected killer of Ukrainian lawmaker Andriy Parubiy admitted on 2 September his role in the killing.
He claimed to have comitted the crime in an act of "revenge" against the country’s authorities.
He denied having worked with Russian special services.

items.title: "I came to be the manager ... not the coach": Manchester United fire head coach Ruben Amorim

s: On Monday, Manchester United football team fired its coach Ruben Amorim after fourteen months in the role.
Amorim had met with Omar Berrada, chief executive officer of the team, and Jason Wilcox, the team's director of football, on Friday morning.
While discussing his preferred 3-4-3 style, the conversation reportedly quickly spiraled out of control, resulting in Amorim losing his job.
Manchester United announced the news of the dismissal at around 10 a.m. on Monday.
After the team drawing against Leeds F.C.
1-1, the coach had said at a press conference that he came to be "the manager, not the coach" and said Wilcox should "do his job".
Wilcox intended the meeting to focus on the recent draw.

Manchester United was sixth in the Premier League, almost not classifying for the Champions League, less than four points ahead of Sunderland A.F.C., Everton F.C., Fulham F.C., Brighton & Hove Albion F.C., Newcastle United and Brentford F.C., a precarious position, El Pais reported.
Former Manchester United captain Gary Neville communicated to Sky Sports News that he expected better performance, saying he "thought they'd get through another couple of weeks."

items.title: Homeland Security says Minneapolis woman shot by ICE officer dies

s: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reported Wednesday that a woman shot by a U.S.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis has died.
Homeland Security officials have described the shooting as an act of self-defense, while Minnesota governor Tim Walz and Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey have pushed back on this account.

DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin stated that the shooting occurred when ICE officers fired "defensive shots" in response to the woman "attempting to run over our law enforcement officers" with her vehicle.
Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said the woman’s conduct was "an act of domestic terrorism."
The incident was under active investigation, with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and the FBI taking over the case.
Walz said the state was working to learn more and asked residents to remain calm, while protest activity continued at the scene and a substantial law-enforcement presence remained in the area.
